theme: Praise the LORD who rebuilds Jerusalem
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 147. Imagine the people standing before the finished wall. Notice who builds, who gathers, and who counts.
settingTheScene: Psalm 147 is one of the five “Hallelujah” psalms that close the Psalter. Verse 2 reads, “The LORD builds up Jerusalem; he gathers the outcasts of Israel.” Many readers connect it to the dedication of the wall in Nehemiah 12. Whether or not it was written for that day, it fits perfectly. It praises the God who builds cities, heals the brokenhearted, counts the stars, and feeds the animals.
observation: “Praise the LORD! For it is good to sing praises to our God” (v. 1).
“The LORD builds up Jerusalem; he gathers the outcasts of Israel” (v. 2).
“He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds” (v. 3).
“He determines the number of the stars; he gives to all of them their names” (v. 4).
“Great is our Lord, and abundant in power; his understanding is beyond measure” (v. 5).
“The LORD lifts up the humble; he casts the wicked to the ground” (v. 6).
“His delight is not in the strength of the horse, nor his pleasure in the legs of a man” (v. 10).
“He declares his word to Jacob, his statutes and rules to Israel” (v. 19).
interpretation:
The psalm gives us a surprising list of what God does, all in the same breath. He builds Jerusalem. He gathers outcasts. He heals the brokenhearted and binds their wounds. And he counts and names every star. The same God who handles the vastness of the cosmos kneels to bandage a wound. There is no contradiction: greatness and tenderness belong together.

This is a good word for a people who had just finished a wall. The wall was built by Nehemiah and the workers, and yet “the LORD builds up Jerusalem.” Our work is real, and God is the true builder (Psalm 127:1).

Verse 6 declares God’s character: he lifts the humble and casts down the wicked. Verses 7 to 9 move to creation: rain on the earth, grass on the hills, food for the beasts and for the young ravens when they cry. God provides for the ravens. If he cares for them, he cares for his people.

Then verse 10 draws a line. He does not delight in the strength of the horse or the legs of a man. He takes pleasure “in those who fear him, in those who hope in his steadfast love.” God is not impressed by human power. He is moved by humble trust.

The psalm ends with the word: God has given his statutes to Israel. “He has not dealt thus with any other nation.” The greatest gift is not military strength or good weather but a God who speaks. The word is what makes the people a people.
connection: Luke 4:18 shows Jesus proclaiming healing for the brokenhearted and release for captives. Matthew 6:26 says the Father feeds the birds of the air. Matthew 10:29-31 teaches that he knows the sparrows and the hairs of our heads. John 10:3 says the shepherd calls his own sheep by name. Isaiah 40:26 also speaks of the God who calls the stars by name. John 1:1: In the beginning was the Word.
application:
Go outside tonight and look at the sky. Thank the God who named the stars and also knows your name.

Name a brokenhearted person you know. Ask God how you might be part of binding up their wounds.

Praise God aloud for his word, which he has given to you.
prayerPrompts: Praise God for rebuilding what is broken.
Thank him that he heals the brokenhearted.
Tell him what has been healed in you.
